_comment: The claims the smoke scenarios prove (#1055). One row per scenario under live/smoke/scenarios/ that is a claim;
import, greenfield and full are demos, not claims, and carry no row. live/smoke_claims_test.go holds this file to the
scenario directory and to the site's per-claim pages, and site/data/claims.json is a byte-for-byte copy the site renders.
substrate names the platform the scenario itself runs on (aws: the floci emulator; kubernetes: a kind cluster); that provider's cell must read proven.
providers.<name>.status is one of: proven (a scenario runs on that substrate and passes), restated (the claim holds in a
different or weaker form, said in note), n/a (the claim's premise does not exist there), open (not yet stated either way).

real_aws: true marks a claim whose scenario cannot run against the emulator honestly and runs against a real AWS account instead. It is maintainer-run (SMOKE_REAL_AWS=1), never CI-gated, and its aws cell reads proven from a maintainer's run recorded in the note, not from CI. live/smoke_claims_test.go holds the flag to the scenario's own refusal.

themes.adopt: Adopt live infrastructure without state surgery
themes.gate: The platform's own policy engine gates every write
themes.cache: The state file is a cache you are allowed to lose

claims.title: The marker is a label: one tofu-estate label on a real cluster
claims.break_mode: BREAK=1 strips the label with kubectl and requires live-ls to drop the object from the listing and the replan to refuse it by name, proposing the create the block declares rather than relabelling an object this estate can no longer show it owns

aws.note: An AWS resource carries two tags, estate and address, because AWS hands back opaque ids; claim 7 proves that shape. The single-label shape exists only where the object's own name is the join key.

claims.title: No silent orphans on Kubernetes: a deleted block's object is found by its label and a controller's copies are never touched
claims.break_mode: BREAK=1 strips the label from the orphan and requires the replan to leave it alone

aws.note: Claim 1 is the AWS shape: one estate-filtered GetResources call over the whole account, and no controller copies labels there.

claims.title: The label is the boundary: the plan refuses another estate's object on its own, and one admission policy fences every write to an estate's objects
claims.break_mode: BREAK=1 removes the policy and requires the writes it refused - Bob's apply and plain kubectl on Alice's estate, and Alice's live-mv -from-estate into an estate she was never granted - to go through, while step 4's plan-side refusal of another estate's object must still hold with the policy gone

aws.note: Claim 13 is the AWS shape: an IAM condition on the ownership tag, which fences reads as well as writes and can name an address, not only an estate.

claims.title: A custom resource binds by its natural key, carries the estate label and is swept by it, a block whose CRD the cluster does not serve is refused by name, and the plan carries the API server's own dry-run verdict on every planned object: a kubernetes_manifest block is found again by the apiVersion, kind, namespace and name inside its manifest, its object is created with tofu-estate in metadata.labels, an object whose block is removed is found by the sweep and proposed for removal, before the CRD is installed the plan refuses the block naming the kind, the apiVersion and the CRD to install, and every planned create or update is sent to the server with dryRun=All and its acceptance printed above the plan, and a custom resource stock created and recorded in a terraform.tfstate is adopted by live-import, which writes that same label as one API merge patch whose dry run is diffed against the live object so a write that would change anything beyond the labels map is refused
claims.break_mode: BREAK=1 writes spec.replicas = 0 under a CRD that bounds it at minimum 1, a rule only the server checks, and requires the replan refused by name with the server's message quoted and no plan produced; strips the tofu-estate label with kubectl and requires the replan to refuse the CronTab by name and the server's dry run to refuse the create it falls back to, leaving the label off until an operator writes it back; strips it again and removes the block, requiring the replan not to list the object; then deletes the custom resource and requires the replan to propose creating it; and it installs a MutatingAdmissionPolicy that rewrites spec.image on every update, then migrates the stock-made CronTab, requiring live-import to refuse the label write by name ("would also change spec.image"), count it as 1 failed, and leave the object's label and spec untouched

aws.note: AWS has no custom-resource shape; every type is a provider type with a schema, and claim 7 proves the marker path for them.

claims.title: A delete the platform accepted but has not finished leaves an object the estate still owns: the object stays with a deletionTimestamp and its marker, the sweep finds it, and every plan proposes the same one destroy until it is really gone
claims.break_mode: BREAK=1 removes the finalizer before the destroying apply and requires the opposite outcome - the object gone in one apply and the replan empty - because without that control the scenario would read identically if choudoufu simply never deleted a ConfigMap

aws.note: No AWS scenario measures this. Most AWS provider deletes wait for the resource to be gone, so the shape is rarer there, but it exists - an eventually-consistent delete, or a DELETE the service accepts and finishes later - and the promise would be the same one: the tag sweep finds a resource that is still there and the next plan proposes it again rather than forgetting it.

claims.title: Admission runs after the plan and the server decides what is stored: a fail-closed webhook's rejection is reported in the API server's own words with nothing changed and the approved plan file still applying unchanged once the webhook answers again, a mutation to a declared field reads as the same perpetual drift stock reads while the estate keeps its marker, and a mutation that strips the marker on the way in is named by the run that made it - the create warns that the marker it sent is not on the object the server stored, and the adopting update that follows fails rather than reporting a change nothing kept
claims.break_mode: BREAK=1 installs the same stripping policy against a DECOY label instead of tofu-estate - identical kind, namespace and JSONPatch, one key different - and requires the opposite outcome: the decoy stripped so the policy is provably in the admission chain and provably mutating, the marker landed, no "Ownership marker was not stored" anywhere in the run, live-ls listing the object as this estate's, and the second apply not wedging on the name; without it the third part would read identically if choudoufu simply never wrote a label, and its two assertions about the marker diagnostic would read identically if that diagnostic fired whatever the server did

aws.note: No AWS scenario measures this. AWS has no admission chain a customer installs, but it has the same two shapes: a service-control or resource policy that refuses a write the plan approved (claim 13 fences writes, it does not measure a refusal arriving after approval), and a service that stores something other than what was sent - a normalised ARN, a default injected by the service, or a tag the account's tag policy rewrites. The third part has a direct AWS counterpart worth proving: an AWS Organizations tag policy can refuse or rewrite the tofu-estate tag on the way in. #1192's hook is substrate-neutral and would report it, but only where the provider hands back the tags it stored rather than the ones it was sent, and that is per resource type and unmeasured.

claims.title: An edit to a Kubernetes object's labels or annotations is an ordinary change: a label edited in the configuration plans one in-place update and the apply writes it, the same answer stock gives for the same edit with a state file behind it, an annotation added and then changed does the same, a label or annotation DELETED from the configuration is removed from the object and the estate then settles, and a key the configuration never declared - the API server's own kubernetes.io/metadata.name, a controller's annotation - stays the server's and churns nothing
claims.break_mode: BREAK=1 runs the identical kubectl command against a key the configuration does NOT declare - same object, same --overwrite, one key different - and requires the opposite outcome, "No changes.", with the label still on the object afterwards. Without it every plan the main arm requires would read the same if choudoufu simply planned on any difference between the configuration and the live object, and step 5's point - that the provider's computed_fields rule still keeps the server's own keys out of the plan - would be scenery.

aws.note: No AWS scenario measures this. The defect it closes is a property of one provider's plan logic rather than of the substrate: hashicorp/kubernetes's kubernetes_manifest reads the PRIOR value of metadata.labels and metadata.annotations to decide whether to keep the live one (its computed_fields argument), and a stateless run has to build that prior. The AWS tag path has no equivalent branch - configuredTagsSeed's prior feeds a provider that diffs tags against configuration directly - so the same edit on an AWS tag has always planned. What is genuinely unproven on AWS is the sibling question step 5 answers on Kubernetes: that a tag a service or another account's automation adds out of band does not churn the plan.
